display.name: Maya Chen
display.blurb: A 24-year-old in her first full-time job: a thin cushion, an employer match, a depegged stablecoin and a self-imposed crypto allowance.

intro: Maya, 24, first full-time job. Take-home pay $2,900 a month (after tax, before any retirement contribution; assumed gross $3,800). Living costs $2,350 a month. Opening: checking $500, savings $1,000, retirement account $2,200. No crypto. Each month-end, anything over $500 in checking is moved to savings automatically.
plan: Starter fund: $3,300 of liquid cash (checking + savings).
Full cushion: $4,700 (two months of living costs).

Crypto allowance: $200 in total until the cushion reaches $4,700, and the starter fund must still be at least $3,300 after any purchase. Once the cushion is $4,700 or more after a purchase, the $200 limit no longer applies.
Order of operations: Reserve, then free money (employer match), then wallet safety, then optional experiments.
Cash in this story is checking + savings only. The retirement account and the vault are not cash.

questions.title: 12%, but your cushion is thin
questions.situation: A coworker shows you a stablecoin yield vault: a crypto service that advertises "up to 12% a year" on a dollar stablecoin (a crypto token designed to stay worth $1). Unlike an insured savings account, a vault deposit is not FDIC-insured. You are saving toward a starter fund and your first laptop replacement.

a.t: Keep your savings where they are.

b.t: Put $300 of savings into the yield vault.

c.t: Put $1,000 of savings into the yield vault.

a.text: You kept your savings. Nothing changed. It earns 100 because your cushion is under your $3,300 starter-fund line, and money you may need soon is not for a vault. "Up to 12%" is an advertised top rate, not a promise. Next: your cash keeps building toward the line.
a.ref: You kept your savings. Nothing changed. It earns 100 because your cushion is under your $3,300 starter-fund line, and money you may need soon is not for a vault. "Up to 12%" is an advertised top rate, not a promise. Next: your cash keeps building toward the line.

b.text: You moved {-d.SAV} into the vault ({d.VAULT} after the fee). Liquid cash is now {post.cash}. It scores 0 because your cushion is already below the starter-fund line. Next: your cash is {-d.SAV} lower in Q2 and Q3, and the vault's value matters again in Q5.
b.ref: You moved $300 into the vault ($298.50 after the fee). Liquid cash is now $1,750. It scores 0 because your cushion is already below the starter-fund line. Next: your cash is $300 lower in Q2 and Q3, and the vault's value matters again in Q5.

c.text: You moved {-d.SAV} into the vault ({d.VAULT} after the fee). Liquid cash is now {post.cash}. It scores 0 for the same reason, at a larger size. Next: much less cash for the car repair and laptop ahead, and a larger vault position in Q5.
c.ref: You moved $1,000 into the vault ($995 after the fee). Liquid cash is now $1,050. It scores 0 for the same reason, at a larger size. Next: much less cash for the car repair and laptop ahead, and a larger vault position in Q5.

questions.takeaway: Build the reserve before chasing yield. A yield offer is not a reason to lend out money you might need.

questions.title: Free money: the employer match
questions.situation: In this story, Maya's employer plan opens. She chooses how much of her pay to contribute. Under this fictional plan the company matches 100% of her contribution, up to 4% of her pay before tax ($3,800 a month). Real employer plans vary: match formulas, eligibility waits and vesting schedules differ, so check the actual plan.

a.t: Contribute 4%. You put in $152, the employer adds $152, and the retirement account receives $304. Your cash falls about $129.20 a month.

b.t: Contribute 2%. $76 from you plus $76 from the employer: $152 into the account; your cash falls about $64.60 a month.

c.t: Contribute 0%. Nothing goes in. You give up $152 a month of employer match.

a.text: You chose 4%. You put in $152, the employer added $152, and {d.RET} went into the retirement account; your cash fell about {-d.cash}. It earns 100 because a 100% match is an immediate return on the money you put in. Next: your cash grows a little slower, which Q3's plan check will show.
a.ref: You chose 4%. You put in $152, the employer added $152, and $304 went into the retirement account; your cash fell about $129.20. It earns 100 because a 100% match is an immediate return on the money you put in. Next: your cash grows a little slower, which Q3's plan check will show.

b.text: You chose 2%, which captures half the match. It scores 100 because your cash after costs is under one month of costs, so protecting liquidity can justify a smaller contribution. You leave $76 a month of match unused. Next: your cash grows faster.
b.ref: You chose 2%, which captures half the match. It scores 100 because your cash after costs is under one month of costs, so protecting liquidity can justify a smaller contribution. You leave $76 a month of match unused. Next: your cash grows faster.

b.text: You chose 2%. It scores 0 because your cash after costs was {pre.cash-2350}, at or above one month of costs, so you could afford the full match and gave up $76 a month. Next: slightly more cash, less in retirement.

c.text: You chose 0%. It scores 0 because you gave up $152 a month of employer money, about $1,976 over the story. Next: more cash now, nothing growing in the plan.
c.ref: You chose 0%. It scores 0 because you gave up $152 a month of employer money, about $1,976 over the story. Next: more cash now, nothing growing in the plan.

questions.takeaway: A match is usually the first return to capture unless cash is too thin to spare the contribution. Retirement money and emergency savings do different jobs.

questions.title: The stablecoin slips to $0.92
questions.lead: A dollar stablecoin is trading at $0.92. No recovery has been announced. Your $900 laptop is due next month. A stablecoin aims to hold $1.00, but nothing guarantees it. Its price depends on what backs it, whether it can be redeemed, and confidence in the issuer. It may recover, stay low or fall further. A vault adds its own risks on top (smart-contract problems, withdrawal limits, the protocol itself), and it is not an insured bank account.

items: none (the stablecoin is in the news; you own none)
